title: Impact of Political Turnover on Public Spending

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy

**Method: Instrumental Variables (IV / 2SLS)**

The research question asks about the causal effect of Democratic control (`x`) on public spending (`y`), but `x` is likely endogenous — localities that elect Democrats may differ systematically in ways that also affect spending (omitted variable bias, reverse causality). 

We use a **close-election Democratic win** (`z`) as an instrument for Democratic control (`x`). This is a classic RDD-inspired IV strategy (à la Lee, Moretti, Butler 2004):

**Key assumptions:**
1. **Relevance:** Close-election Democratic wins predict Democratic control (strong first stage). Winning a close election shifts the probability of Democratic governance.
2. **Independence/Exogeneity:** In close elections, the winner is essentially randomly assigned — the instrument is as-good-as-random conditional on controls.
3. **Exclusion Restriction:** A close-election Democratic win affects public spending *only* through its effect on Democratic control, not through other channels.
4. **Monotonicity (LATE):** Winning a close election does not cause any unit to have *less* Democratic control.

## 2. R Code

```r
# ============================================================
# IV / 2SLS Analysis: Effect of Democratic Control on Spending
# ============================================================

# Load required packages
if (!require("AER")) install.packages("AER", repos="https://cloud.r-project.org")
if (!require("lmtest")) install.packages("lmtest", repos="https://cloud.r-project.org")
if (!require("sandwich")) install.packages("sandwich", repos="https://cloud.r-project.org")

library(AER)
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# ---------------------------
# 1. Load and inspect data
# ---------------------------
df <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s74_data.csv")
cat("=== Data Summary ===\n")
cat("Dimensions:", nrow(df), "x", ncol(df), "\n\n")
summary(df)
cat("\nCorrelations:\n")
print(cor(df))

# ---------------------------
# 2. OLS Benchmark (Naive)
# ---------------------------
cat("\n\n========== OLS (Naive) Estimation ==========\n")
ols_model <- lm(y ~ x + controls, data = df)
cat("\nOLS Results:\n")
print(summary(ols_model))

# OLS with robust standard errors
cat("\nOLS with Robust SEs:\n")
print(coeftest(ols_model, vcov = vcovHC(ols_model, type = "HC1")))

# ---------------------------
# 3. First Stage: z -> x
# ---------------------------
cat("\n\n========== First Stage: x ~ z + controls ==========\n")
first_stage <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = df)
print(summary(first_stage))

# First-stage F-statistic on excluded instrument
fs_fstat <- (summary(first_stage)$coefficients["z", "t value"])^2
cat("\nFirst-stage F-statistic on excluded instrument z:", round(fs_fstat, 2), "\n")
if (fs_fstat > 10) {
  cat("=> Strong instrument (F > 10, Stock-Yogo threshold).\n")
} else {
  cat("=> WARNING: Potentially weak instrument (F < 10).\n")
}

# ---------------------------
# 4. IV / 2SLS Estimation
# ---------------------------
cat("\n\n========== IV / 2SLS Estimation ==========\n")
iv_model <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = df)
cat("\nIV (2SLS) Results:\n")
print(summary(iv_model, diagnostics = TRUE))

# IV with robust standard errors
cat("\nIV with Robust Standard Errors (HC1):\n")
iv_robust <- coeftest(iv_model, vcov = vcovHC(iv_model, type = "HC1"))
print(iv_robust)

# ---------------------------
# 5. Compare OLS vs IV
# ---------------------------
cat("\n\n========== Comparison: OLS vs IV ==========\n")
ols_coef <- coef(ols_model)["x"]
iv_coef  <- coef(iv_model)["x"]
cat("OLS coefficient on x (Democratic control):", round(ols_coef, 4), "\n")
cat("IV  coefficient on x (Democratic control):", round(iv_coef, 4), "\n")
cat("Difference (IV - OLS):", round(iv_coef - ols_coef, 4), "\n")

# ---------------------------
# 6. Robustness Checks
# ---------------------------
cat("\n\n========== Robustness Checks ==========\n")

# 6a. Reduced Form: z -> y (intent-to-treat)
cat("\n--- Reduced Form (ITT): y ~ z + controls ---\n")
reduced_form <- lm(y ~ z + controls, data = df)
print(summary(reduced_form))

rf_coef <- coef(reduced_form)["z"]
fs_coef <- coef(first_stage)["z"]
cat("Wald/IV estimate (reduced form / first stage):", round(rf_coef / fs_coef, 4), "\n")
cat("2SLS estimate:", round(iv_coef, 4), "\n")

# 6b. IV without controls (sensitivity)
cat("\n--- IV without controls ---\n")
iv_nocontrols <- ivreg(y ~ x | z, data = df)
print(summary(iv_nocontrols, diagnostics = TRUE))

# 6c. Hausman test (endogeneity test)
cat("\n--- Hausman-type Endogeneity Test ---\n")
# Manual approach: include first-stage residuals in OLS
df$fs_resid <- residuals(first_stage)
hausman_test <- lm(y ~ x + controls + fs_resid, data = df)
hausman_pval <- summary(hausman_test)$coefficients["fs_resid", "Pr(>|t|)"]
cat("Coefficient on first-stage residual:", 
    round(coef(hausman_test)["fs_resid"], 4), "\n")
cat("p-value:", round(hausman_pval, 4), "\n")
if (hausman_pval < 0.05) {
  cat("=> Reject exogeneity of x at 5% level. IV is preferred over OLS.\n")
} else {
  cat("=> Cannot reject exogeneity of x. OLS may be consistent.\n")
}

# ---------------------------
# 7. Key Summary
# ---------------------------
cat("\n\n========================================\n")
cat("         FINAL SUMMARY\n")
cat("========================================\n")
cat("First-stage F-stat:", round(fs_fstat, 2), "\n")
cat("OLS estimate (x on y):", round(ols_coef, 4), "\n")
cat("IV estimate  (x on y):", round(iv_coef, 4), "\n")
cat("IV robust SE:", round(iv_robust["x", "Std. Error"], 4), "\n")
cat("IV robust p-value:", round(iv_robust["x", "Pr(>|t|)"], 4), "\n")
cat("========================================\n")
```

## 3. Expected Findings

**Expected sign and magnitude:**

- **First stage:** The instrument `z` (close-election Democratic win) should have a **positive and statistically significant** effect on `x` (Democratic control), with an F-statistic well above 10, confirming instrument relevance.

- **IV coefficient on `x`:** I expect a **positive** coefficient, indicating that Democratic control increases public spending. The magnitude likely falls in the range of **0.3–0.8** (in log points), meaning a one-unit increase in Democratic control is associated with a 30–80% increase in public spending.

- **OLS vs. IV comparison:** The OLS estimate may be **attenuated** (biased toward zero) due to measurement error in Democratic control, or **biased upward** if unobserved demand for public goods drives both Democratic voting and spending. The IV estimate corrects for this endogeneity, and the Hausman test will indicate whether the difference is statistically significant.

- **Reduced form:** The direct effect of `z` on `y` should be positive and significant, confirming the intent-to-treat effect. The Wald ratio (reduced form ÷ first stage) should match the 2SLS estimate exactly.

- **Robustness:** Results should be qualitatively similar with and without controls, and the diagnostic tests from `ivreg` (Wu-Hausman, Sargan if applicable) should support the validity of the IV approach.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Use close-election Democratic wins as an instrument for Democratic control.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The analysis suggests a negative causal impact of Democratic control on public spending.
